newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Surprise fall in Zimbabwe inflation.
newsitem.headline: Surprise fall in Zimbabwe inflation.

text.p: Zimbabwe's year-on-year inflation rate dipped to a three-year low of just under 18 percent in August, surprising many economic analysts who were expecting it to track upward on a spate of price rises.
August's year-on-year consumer price index (CPI) stood at 17.7 percent compared to 22 percent in July, largely due to a fall in food prices, the analysts said on Tuesday.
"Food prices have a significant weighting on the total inflation basket, they comprise 29 percent of the total inflation basket," said private economic analyst Eric Bloch.

"They (food prices) are substantially lower now -- between 35 and 40 percent -- from last year and that's the single biggest factor behind the fall in inflation in August," he told Reuters, Zimbabwe had a bumper harvest this year following last year's drought.

However, other economists -- such as Farai Zizhou of the Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) and Edmore Tobaiwa of the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce -- said they had not expected such a big fall in August inflation.

"Even taking into account the weighting of food on the CPI basket, the fall in staple food prices was not that high to warrant such a decrease in inflation," said an analyst with a local commercial bank, adding: "I would have expected it to fall to not less than 20 percent," he added.
The analyst, who asked not to be named, and Zizhou said they had expected annual inflation to rise in August and September due to increases in energy and milk prices announced in July.
They said they would now have to revise their forecasts for inflation for the end of the year and for mid-1997.

Central Reserve Bank Governor Leonard Tsumba has said he expected fuel price rises announced in July and recent wage hikes in the private and public sectors to push inflation to between 23 and 24 percent in the next two months before easing to 20 percent by December.
Civil servants won large pay rises recently by bringing the country to a near standstill through widespread strikes.
"Depending on fiscal performance and, of course, on the 1996/97 rainy season, inflation should decline further to about 17 percent by the end of June 1997," Tsumbe said this month.
He and other Reserve Bank officials were unavailable for comment on the latest inflation statistics.

Stock brokers and analysts said on Tuesday this latest fall in annual inflation should bolster sentiment on the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange, which has been on a heady bull-run on prospects of lower interest rates and further investment incentives for the exchange.

"The fall in inflation which fuels hopes for cuts in interest rates makes the stock exchange a much more attractive home for investment as opposed to the money market because the returns there will be lower," said a broker.
